label: Atco
description: The Los Angeles quintet's debut pairs Stephen Stills and Richie Furay's ringing, Byrds-indebted folk rock with Neil Young's first songs on record, including 'Burned' and 'Out of My Mind.' The record is mostly clean and pretty, built on twin guitars and close vocal blend, but it is where Young's reedy voice and restless writing first show up. It matters here as a root of what came downstream: Young's solo career, CSNY and Poco.
lineage: Formed in LA in 1966 by Stephen Stills, Richie Furay and Neil Young (with Bruce Palmer and Dewey Martin); the band is the shared origin point for Young's solo career, CSNY, and Poco.

label: Atco
description: Each of the band's three songwriters got room to stretch on this second LP: Stills's 'Bluebird' and 'Rock & Roll Woman,' Furay's country-leaning 'A Child's Claim to Fame,' and Young's 'Mr. Soul,' the orchestrated 'Expecting to Fly' and the multi-part collage 'Broken Arrow.' It is more ambitious and more fractured than the debut, cut in pieces as the band's internal tension grew. The Young songs already sound like a solo artist auditioning inside someone else's band.
lineage: Buffalo Springfield's most ambitious record, made as the band was already splintering; 'Broken Arrow' sounds like an early sketch of the song-suite instincts Young would later pursue on records like Greendale.

label: Atco
description: Assembled from leftover sessions after the band had effectively broken up, with the members rarely in a room together, this closing LP leans toward Furay's country-rock instincts (pedal steel on 'Kind Woman') even as Young contributes 'On the Way Home' and the fragile 'I Am a Child.' It is looser and sadder than the first two records, a band's epitaph rather than a statement. Furay and Jim Messina would carry the country-rock half of this sound straight into Poco.
lineage: Buffalo Springfield's farewell record, split between Furay's country-rock turn (feeding directly into Poco) and Young's folk songs, which sound like a preview of his solo debut the same year.

label: Reprise
description: Young's first solo album is a lush, string-and-woodwind-laden folk-rock record, shaped by Jack Nitzsche's orchestral arrangements rather than the ragged band sound he would soon build with Crazy Horse. Songs like 'The Loner' and 'The Old Laughing Lady' already carry his strange, reedy phrasing even under all the studio polish. It sets out the moody, wandering songwriting he would spend the next decade refining.
lineage: Young's solo launch straight out of Buffalo Springfield, still wearing 1960s orchestral-pop production before Crazy Horse stripped the sound down.
key_tracks: Here We Are in the Years

label: Reprise
description: Young's second solo album is the true beginning of this lane: his first record with Danny Whitten, Billy Talbot and Ralph Molina as Crazy Horse, cut fast and loose after the orchestral polish of the debut. 'Cinnamon Girl,' 'Down by the River' and 'Cowgirl in the Sand' were reportedly written in a single feverish afternoon, and the two long tracks stretch out into raw, one-note guitar solos that became Young's signature. It is the blueprint for every long, fuzzy, half-in-tune guitar jam that follows in this lane.
lineage: The founding document of the Neil Young/Crazy Horse sound, with Danny Whitten's rhythm guitar setting the template that feeds everything from Zuma through Ragged Glory to Wednesday and MJ Lenderman decades later.

label: Reprise
description: Recorded mostly at Young's home studio with a shifting cast including Stephen Stills and a very young Nils Lofgren on piano, this is the quiet, high, cracked-voice side of Young's writing: 'Only Love Can Break Your Heart,' 'Tell Me Why,' and the title track's strange, apocalyptic imagery over simple piano chords. 'Southern Man' is the record's one loud detour, a fuzzy electric protest song that Lynyrd Skynyrd would later answer. It set the template for the acoustic, plainspoken side of Young that keeps resurfacing across his catalog.
lineage: Young's move from Crazy Horse's electric sprawl to hushed piano-and-guitar songwriting, a direct ancestor of the folk side of this whole lane and of records like Harvest and Comes a Time.
key_tracks: Only Love Can Break Your Heart

label: Reprise
description: Young's commercial peak, cut partly in Nashville with the Stray Gators (Ben Keith's pedal steel is all over it) and partly with a full orchestra in London for 'A Man Needs a Maid' and 'There's a World.' 'Heart of Gold' went to number one and made Young a reluctant star, something he'd spend the rest of the decade running from. It is the most straightforwardly pretty record in this catalog, the country-folk side of the lane at its most polished.
lineage: The commercial high point of Young's country-folk side, cut with the same Nashville pedal-steel band sound as Harvest Moon two decades later; its success is the thing Tonight's the Night and On the Beach deliberately reject.
key_tracks: The Needle and the Damage Done

label: Reprise
description: Recorded live on the disastrous, drug-strained 1973 tour that followed Harvest's success, with a band that barely rehearsed the new songs before playing them to arenas expecting more 'Heart of Gold.' None of these songs were ever released in studio versions, which makes the record feel like a document of a breakdown in real time, all ragged edges and cracked high notes. It is the first record of what fans call Young's 'ditch trilogy,' turning hard away from the polish that made him famous.
lineage: Commonly grouped as the opening record of Young's 'ditch trilogy,' made after Harvest's mainstream success and sharing its ragged, unpolished mood with On the Beach and Tonight's the Night.

label: Reprise
description: The second leg of the ditch trilogy, cut with a loose, murky sound that matches its hungover mood. 'Revolution Blues' is a menacing song written in the voice of a Manson-like cult leader, while the closing 'Ambulance Blues' rambles for close to nine minutes over a simple acoustic figure. It is one of the bleakest, least commercial records Young released on a major label, and exactly the record Harvest's audience did not want.
lineage: The middle of the 'ditch trilogy,' recorded in deliberate retreat from Harvest's success and sharing its hungover, unpolished mood with Tonight's the Night, recorded around the same period.

label: Reprise
description: Recorded in 1973 but held back for two years, this is Young's grief record for two friends who died of heroin overdoses: Crazy Horse guitarist Danny Whitten and roadie Bruce Berry. The vocals are shredded, off-key and barely holding together on songs like the title track and 'Tired Eyes.' It is the rawest, least polished record in this catalog, more a wake caught on tape than a finished album.
lineage: Young's bleakest record, made in mourning for Danny Whitten with Crazy Horse's rhythm section; its ragged, barely-in-control sound seems an ancestor of the loose, live-in-the-room ethic this atlas keeps returning to.

label: Reprise
description: Crazy Horse's first record after Danny Whitten's death, with Frank 'Poncho' Sampedro joining on rhythm guitar in a lineup that would last for decades. The long, slow-building 'Cortez the Killer' is the centerpiece, a patient lead-guitar showcase over a loping groove. After two bleak ditch-trilogy records, Zuma sounds like the band finding its footing again, still ragged but warmer and more open.
lineage: The record where the classic four-piece Crazy Horse lineup (Young, Talbot, Molina, Sampedro) locks into place, the same lineup behind Ragged Glory and Sleeps with Angels.

label: Reprise
description: A patchwork record stitched from several different sessions, pairing rowdy honky-tonk numbers cut with a country band (Emmylou Harris sings harmony on several tracks) with a leftover Crazy Horse cut and the solo acoustic 'Will to Love.' The mismatched sequencing gives it a loose, tossed-off feel, but 'Like a Hurricane,' with its long, droning guitar solo over a wash of organ, is one of Young's most enduring live staples. It sits right at the crossroads of the country and Crazy Horse sides of this lane.
lineage: A grab-bag that sums up the whole V20 lane in one record: honky-tonk numbers with Emmylou Harris singing harmony on one side, a distorted Crazy Horse epic on the other.

label: Reprise
description: A warm, mostly acoustic country-folk record built around close vocal harmonies with Nicolette Larson, who sings on much of the album, including the duet 'Lotta Love' and the cover 'Four Strong Winds.' The arrangements are gentle and unhurried, with fiddle and acoustic guitars up front. It is the gentlest record between Zuma and Rust Never Sleeps, closer in spirit to Harvest than to Crazy Horse.
lineage: The clearest bridge between Harvest's Nashville-pop side and Harvest Moon a decade and a half later, with Nicolette Larson's harmonies doing what Emmylou Harris's did on American Stars 'n Bars.

label: Reprise
description: Split cleanly down the middle, side one solo acoustic and side two full-volume Crazy Horse, the record bookends itself with 'My My, Hey Hey (Out of the Blue)' and its electric twin 'Hey Hey, My My (Into the Black),' the songs that gave punk-era Young the line 'it's better to burn out than to fade away.' 'Powderfinger,' a narrative death ballad, sits at the album's emotional center. Assembled from a 1978 tour with a stage set built to look like giant amps and roadies dressed as hooded 'road-eyes,' it is Young's most theatrical statement of the two sides of his sound.
lineage: The record that most explicitly states this lane's whole thesis, an acoustic folk side and a distorted Crazy Horse side on one LP, cited for decades by punk and grunge musicians as proof Young never went soft.
key_tracks: My My, Hey Hey (Out of the Blue)
Hey Hey, My My (Into the Black)

label: Reprise
description: The full-length concert document of the same 1978 tour that produced Rust Never Sleeps, pairing solo acoustic renditions with extended, feedback-drenched Crazy Horse jams on 'Cortez the Killer' and 'Like a Hurricane.' It captures the theatrical stage show, with giant amps and road crew dressed as hooded 'road-eyes.' As a document of the band stretching out in real time, it is some of the purest recorded evidence of the Crazy Horse jam at full length.
lineage: The concert-length companion to Rust Never Sleeps, showing the acoustic/electric split of that record played out live at length.

label: Reprise
description: A brief, patchwork record split between leftover mellow acoustic songs from the mid-1970s and a handful of new, flag-waving country tunes, including the title track's blunt, almost jingoistic patriotism. It runs under 30 minutes and reads more like a transitional sketch than a statement. The fiddle-and-harmony country side points toward the Nashville detours Young would take later in the decade.
lineage: A minor, transitional record that shows Young's country-folk side turning overtly political, a mood that resembles the one he'd revisit decades later on Living with War.

label: Reprise
description: A blunt, repetitive, almost mechanical Crazy Horse record, made during a hard stretch in Young's family life. 'T-Bone' repeats essentially one line about mashed potatoes for nine minutes over a churning riff. It is one of the least song-oriented, most purely textural records in the catalog, closer to proto-noise-rock than anything else Young made in this period.
lineage: The most repetitive, riff-obsessed Crazy Horse record, sounding like a forerunner of the noise and drone experiments Young would return to on Arc a decade later.

label: Geffen
description: Young's strangest detour, built around vocoder-processed vocals and synthesizers, made in part while he was trying to find a way to communicate with his nonverbal son. It confused his label and audience at the time and began the run of genre-hopping Geffen records that ended in the label suing him. Heard now, it plays like an outsider new-wave record more than a Crazy Horse album, proof of how far Young was willing to stretch the sound.
lineage: The most electronic record in Young's catalog and the first of his Geffen genre detours; it sounds like a strange cousin to the drum-machine and synth experiments on indie music's country-adjacent fringes.

artist: Neil Young and the Shocking Pinks
label: Geffen
description: A short, deliberately retro rockabilly pastiche, cut with a new backing band (the Shocking Pinks) doing 1950s-style slap-bass and doo-wop harmonies, clocking in under 25 minutes. It was another entry in the run of genre experiments that prompted Geffen's lawsuit against Young for delivering music 'unrepresentative' of his usual sound. It's a minor, oddball record, but it shows the same restlessness that runs through Trans and Old Ways, Young refusing to repeat himself even at commercial cost.
lineage: Part of Young's contrarian early-80s run of genre exercises for Geffen, sandwiched between the synth-pop of Trans and the straight country of Old Ways.

label: Geffen
description: A straight-up Nashville country record with pedal steel and fiddle throughout and guest vocals from Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson, closer to outlaw country than anything else Young made. It is the most fully realized of his Geffen-era genre detours. A minor record in his catalog but a real data point for how directly this lane touches outlaw and honky-tonk country.
lineage: Young's most straightforward country record, cut with Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson, connecting this lane directly to outlaw country's Nashville mainstream.
key_tracks: Are There Any More Real Cowboys?

label: Geffen
description: A harsh, drum-machine-and-synth-driven rock record from his least-loved commercial period. It has little of the loose Crazy Horse feel; the production is cold, digital and very mid-1980s, with Young's voice pushed into a shouted upper register on songs like 'Hippie Dream.' It is included here mainly as a completist marker of how far this artist could stray from the sound this lane is built around.
lineage: A low ebb of Young's 1980s wandering, directly preceding his return to Crazy Horse on Life the following year.

label: Geffen
description: Crazy Horse's first Neil Young studio record since Re-ac-tor, though the 1980s production (gated drums, synth pads) sits oddly over the band's usual raw sound. 'Mideast Vacation' and 'Long Walk Home' carry blunt political commentary about the Reagan era. It is a transitional, imperfect record, but it is the hinge between the Geffen years and the band's full-force comeback on Ragged Glory three years later.
lineage: Crazy Horse's return to a Neil Young studio album after Re-ac-tor, still burdened by 80s production but pointing the way back to the raw sound of Ragged Glory.

label: Reprise
description: A horn-driven blues-and-R&B record cut with a big band called the Bluenotes, built around the title track's blunt swipe at rock stars doing beer and soda commercials. It is an outlier in this catalog stylistically, more bar-band blues than Crazy Horse fuzz. Still, it shows the same restless, contrarian streak that runs through Young's late-1980s return to Reprise.
lineage: One of Young's genre-hopping detours back at Reprise, swapping Crazy Horse's guitars for a horn section, with a blunt, contrarian streak that resembles Living with War almost twenty years later.

label: Reprise
description: Young's comeback record after a wandering decade, bookended by acoustic and electric versions of 'Rockin' in the Free World,' the song that became his signature protest anthem. The record mixes solo acoustic tracks with full-band, occasionally Crazy Horse-adjacent noise, and it sounds like Young reclaiming his own voice after the Geffen years. It set up the next decade of alternating loud and quiet records that defines this lane.
lineage: The record where Young reclaims his own template after a decade of genre experiments, its acoustic/electric 'Rockin' in the Free World' bookends echoing Rust Never Sleeps a decade earlier.

label: Reprise
description: Recorded live off the floor at Young's ranch, this is Crazy Horse at maximum volume and maximum sprawl, several tracks running past ten minutes of distorted, barely-in-tune guitar interplay. It landed just as grunge was breaking, and Sonic Youth opened the arena tour that followed. It is the clearest single-album distillation of the 'Crazy Horse fuzz' this whole lane is built around.
lineage: Sonic Youth opened the tour behind it, and its roaring guitar sound resembles and seems to have emboldened Dinosaur Jr. and the 1990s noisy-guitar underground.

label: Reprise
description: A double live album from the Ragged Glory tour, with Sonic Youth opening, capturing Crazy Horse at its loudest and most extended, with 'Like a Hurricane' and 'Cortez the Killer' stretched into long, feedback-soaked workouts. It was originally packaged with the companion noise collage Arc, framing feedback itself as part of the performance. It is the sound of an older band matching the young noise-rock bands that sound built in its image.
lineage: The live document of the Ragged Glory tour, on which Sonic Youth opened; its extended, feedback-heavy guitar rock resembles and seems to have encouraged the early-1990s alternative scene.

label: Reprise
description: A roughly 35-minute collage of feedback, amp hum and song fragments edited together from the Ragged Glory tour, originally sold packaged with the live album Weld. It has almost no conventional songwriting on it at all, just texture, drone and distortion, making it Young's most explicitly avant-garde release. It reads as an unlikely handshake between a 1960s folk-rock veteran and the noise underground he was touring alongside.
lineage: Young's pure noise experiment, assembled from Ragged Glory tour feedback while Sonic Youth were opening the shows; it sounds closer to the noise-rock underground than to anything else in his catalog.

label: Reprise
description: A deliberate, twenty-years-later sequel to Harvest, reuniting the Stray Gators musicians (Ben Keith's pedal steel again central) for a warm, mostly acoustic country-folk record. It arrived at the height of grunge, an unfashionable, unhurried move that still connected with a large audience. Songs like 'Unknown Legend' and 'From Hank to Hendrix' explicitly look backward, tying the catalog's threads together.
lineage: A direct, self-aware sequel to Harvest with the same Nashville-pedal-steel band, showing the country-folk half of this lane at its most comfortable and popular.

label: Reprise
description: Young's MTV Unplugged set, recorded acoustic with a small band including Nicolette Larson and Ben Keith, reworking songs from across his catalog including a 'Like a Hurricane' recast on pump organ. It is one of the more purely pretty documents of the acoustic, country-folk side of this lane, sequenced almost like a career overview. Gentle tempos and harmony vocals keep the whole set warm and unhurried.
lineage: A career-spanning acoustic overview that puts the quiet, country-folk half of Young's catalog (Harvest, Comes a Time, After the Gold Rush) side by side in one set.

label: Reprise
description: Recorded in the shadow of Kurt Cobain's death (Cobain had quoted 'it's better to burn out than to fade away' in his suicide note), this is a hushed, mournful, occasionally still very loud Crazy Horse record, split between quiet dirges and the sprawling 'Change Your Mind.' The mood is heavier and more grief-stricken than Ragged Glory, closer in spirit to Tonight's the Night's wake-like atmosphere. It is one of the most emotionally weighted records in the whole catalog.
lineage: A grief record shadowed by Kurt Cobain's death and his quotation of Young's own lyric, closing a loop between Young's influence on grunge and grunge's cost.

label: Reprise
description: Young backed by Pearl Jam rather than Crazy Horse, cut live off the floor in a handful of days with almost no overdubs, the raw production leaving songs ending in unplanned feedback and count-offs. Eddie Vedder sings lead on one track ('Peace and Love'), and the whole record sounds like a grunge-era update of the Ragged Glory formula with a younger band supplying the muscle. It is the clearest single document of Young's direct hand in shaping the sound of the bands he'd influenced.
lineage: Young backed by Pearl Jam instead of Crazy Horse, making explicit the influence line running from Ragged Glory into 1990s grunge.

label: Reprise
description: A loose, sometimes shambolic Crazy Horse record that closes with a murky bar-room recording of a Jimmy Reed cover. It leans further into deliberate rawness than even Ragged Glory, with long, meandering solos on 'Big Time' and 'Slip Away' that sound closer to a rehearsal tape than a finished master. Its unfinished quality is the draw for longtime Young listeners.
lineage: Crazy Horse pushing deliberate looseness even further than Ragged Glory; its lo-fi bar-tape closer sounds like an ancestor of the DIY-recording ethic prized elsewhere in this atlas.

label: Reprise
description: A live album (and companion Jim Jarmusch concert film) from the 1996 Broken Arrow tour, leaning into long, loose, sometimes shaggy extended jams rather than tight renditions. Jarmusch's accompanying black-and-white film was shot in deliberately gritty, unglamorous 16mm, matching the record's rough-edged mood. It's a minor entry compared to Weld or Live Rust, valued mostly by committed fans for how far the band was willing to stretch songs in concert.
lineage: A shaggier companion to Weld, capturing Crazy Horse's mid-90s live sound and its ongoing appeal to filmmakers and musicians drawn to its unpolished, in-the-room feel.

label: Reprise
description: Cut without Neil Young while Danny Whitten was still alive, this is the band's own debut, featuring Whitten's own compositions (including 'I Don't Want to Talk About It,' later covered by Rod Stewart and Everything but the Girl) and Nils Lofgren, then a teenager, on piano and guitar. It's gentler and more song-based than the records the band would make backing Young, closer to Laurel Canyon soft rock than to the fuzz-heavy jams to come. Whitten's death the following year makes this record a bittersweet document of what the band might have become on its own.
lineage: The band's own debut while Danny Whitten was still alive, giving the Crazy Horse name and sound an identity independent of Neil Young before Whitten's 1972 death.
key_tracks: I Don't Want to Talk About It

label: Reprise
description: The band's second album, made after Danny Whitten's departure, with new guitarists stepping in and leaning into looser, jammier arrangements than the debut. It is one of the least discussed records in the whole Crazy Horse orbit, but it shows the rhythm section of Billy Talbot and Ralph Molina, the band's true constant, holding the group together through a lineup crisis. A minor, transitional record but a real link between the debut and the band's later independent efforts.
lineage: Crazy Horse regrouping after Danny Whitten's exit, with Talbot and Molina as the constant thread that would carry the band through decades of Neil Young albums and its own occasional records.

label: Epic
description: The band's third album and first on a different label (Epic rather than Reprise), continuing the loose, mid-tempo rock sound of Loose without Neil Young's involvement. It is a minor, little-remembered record, notable mostly as evidence of how hard the rhythm section of Talbot and Molina kept trying to sustain Crazy Horse as its own band. The group would not release another album under its own name for six years.
lineage: A minor, independent Crazy Horse record from the band's early-1970s attempt to sustain a career apart from Neil Young.

label: RCA
description: A late-1970s return of the Crazy Horse name on yet another label (RCA), leaning on Billy Talbot and Ralph Molina's steady rhythm section with a rotating cast of guitarists. It arrived the same year as Young's own Comes a Time, and its straightforward mid-tempo rock shows the band's persistence in building an identity outside its most famous employer. Like the band's other standalone records, it is mostly for Young completists.
lineage: Another attempt by Talbot and Molina to sustain Crazy Horse as an independent band, arriving the same year as Young's own Comes a Time.

label: Heyday
description: A late Crazy Horse album under the band's own name, cut on an independent label the same year Young released Freedom. It is a low-budget, little-heard record, more a curio for completists than an essential entry, with plain, workmanlike rock arrangements. Talbot and Molina remain the constant across all of these self-directed records, just as they remain the constant across decades of Neil Young albums.
lineage: A Crazy Horse album made apart from Neil Young, part of the band's parallel independent career just before its work with Young entered its 1990s renaissance.

label: Atlantic
description: Neil Young's first album as a full member of CSN, adding his songs ('Helpless' and the 'Country Girl' suite) and his guitar to their close three- and four-part harmonies. It is a Laurel Canyon landmark that fused folk-rock harmony singing with harder electric guitar than CSN alone had used. Young's presence pulls the sound toward the ragged, guitar-forward end of the spectrum compared with the group's smoother 1969 debut.
lineage: David Crosby, Stephen Stills and Graham Nash's trio expanded to include Neil Young, straight out of the same Los Angeles folk-rock world that produced Buffalo Springfield and the Byrds.

label: Atlantic
description: A sprawling double live album pairing the group's acoustic close-harmony sets with much harder electric jamming, including an extended, Crazy Horse-adjacent 'Southern Man' that runs well past ten minutes. It captures the group at its most fractious and its most powerful simultaneously, right before the original quartet's long, on-and-off breakup began in earnest. The electric side previews how far Young would push the loud half of his sound once he left the group behind for Crazy Horse full-time.
lineage: The quartet's live document showing the acoustic-harmony and electric-jam halves of the CSNY sound side by side, a split that resembles the one Young would use again on Rust Never Sleeps.

label: Reprise
description: A duo record between Stephen Stills and Neil Young that began life as a planned Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young reunion before Crosby and Nash's vocals were stripped off and Young abruptly quit the tour partway through, leaving only a cryptic telegram behind by way of explanation. What's left is a warm, mid-tempo country-rock record anchored by the title track, an ode to Young's old hearse. It's a strange, half-finished-feeling footnote, but it's a direct line back to the original Buffalo Springfield partnership.
lineage: A Stills/Young reunion assembled from an aborted CSNY comeback, the last time this particular Buffalo Springfield pairing worked together before decades of on-and-off CSNY activity.

label: Atlantic
description: The full quartet's first studio reunion in eighteen years, cut with glossy, very-1988 production (synth pads and gated drums) that dates it more than almost anything else in this catalog. Young's songs, including the title track and 'Name of Love,' bring some sharper political bite to an otherwise soft-rock record. It is not a fan favorite for any of the four members, but it is a real data point in the group's long on-and-off history.
lineage: The full quartet's belated studio reunion after Déjà Vu, arriving the same late-80s stretch as Young's own wandering Geffen-era records.

label: Reprise
description: The quartet's final studio album together, moved to Young's own label Reprise and leaning more acoustic and song-driven than American Dream's glossy 1980s production. Young contributes several of the record's stronger tracks, including 'Slowpoke' and the title song, while the group's harmony blend, by now three decades old, remains the record's clearest strength. It closed out CSNY's studio career on a quieter, more graceful note than the group had managed in years.
lineage: The last CSNY studio album, closing a three-decade-long, on-and-off partnership that started with Déjà Vu and traces back to Buffalo Springfield and the Byrds.

label: Reprise
description: A quiet, largely acoustic record built from songs Young had been sitting on for years, some dating back to the Harvest Moon and Unplugged era, with Ben Keith's pedal steel again anchoring the sound. It is gentle almost to a fault, closer in spirit to Comes a Time than to anything loud, arriving as a deliberate change of pace after the noisier Year of the Horse. 'Daddy Went Walkin'' and 'Distant Camera' show Young turning reflective and domestic as he moved into his fifties.
lineage: A late entry in the quiet, pedal-steel-driven country-folk lineage running from Harvest through Comes a Time and Harvest Moon.

label: Reprise
description: A concept record and accompanying film telling a loose, multi-generational story about a fictional California town called Greendale, sung mostly in character and stretched out with long, repetitive Crazy Horse grooves under the narrative. It is one of the most overtly storytelling-driven records in Young's catalog, closer to a folk opera than a normal album, touching on media, the environment and small-town life. It pushes the 'ragged guitar plus plainspoken story' idea that runs through this lane about as far as it can go.
lineage: Young's most explicit storytelling concept record, sounding like his earlier multi-part songwriting ('Broken Arrow') stretched into a full small-town saga with Crazy Horse underneath.

label: Reprise
description: Recorded in Nashville shortly before surgery for a brain aneurysm, with Emmylou Harris singing harmony and a return to the pedal-steel, string-and-horn arrangements of Harvest and Harvest Moon. Songs like 'Far from Home' and 'This Old Guitar' are openly reflective about mortality and family history, giving the record a valedictory feel. It is sometimes grouped with Harvest and Harvest Moon as the gentlest chapter of an informal trilogy.
lineage: Often grouped with Harvest and Harvest Moon, with Emmylou Harris on harmony and the same pedal-steel country-folk sound as those records.

label: Reprise
description: A fast, blunt protest record against the Iraq War and the Bush administration, cut in about two weeks with a 100-voice choir and a trumpet player standing in for a guitar solo on several tracks. 'Let's Impeach the President' is as direct as protest songwriting gets, naming its target outright over a driving rock arrangement. It's one of the most overtly political records in his catalog, continuing a streak of topical songwriting that runs back through Ohio and Southern Man.
lineage: A blunt-force protest record in the direct lineage of 'Ohio' and 'Southern Man,' Young's political songwriting turned all the way up against the Iraq War.

label: Reprise
description: A sequel in name only to the long-unreleased 1977 Chrome Dreams, mixing choir and horn arrangements with the sprawling, eighteen-minute guitar showcase 'Ordinary People,' a song Young had been sitting on since the 1980s. It is a genuinely varied record, jumping between styles more than most of his 2000s output, and 'Ordinary People' stretches the Crazy Horse-style solo to its limit. It shares only a title with the original Chrome Dreams, which did not see official release until 2023.
lineage: A stylistic grab-bag that borrows its name from the legendary unreleased 1977 Chrome Dreams while extending the long-solo, horn-and-choir experiments of Young's mid-2000s work.

label: Reprise
description: A stark solo-electric record produced by Daniel Lanois, who wrapped Young's guitar and voice in loops, echo and dub-style processing rather than a full band, so the record sounds like Crazy Horse's fuzz distilled down to one guitar and a room full of reverb. Songs like 'Hitchhiker' and 'Angry World' are largely just Young alone with his instrument, made huge and strange through Lanois's studio treatment. One of the more unusual late-career reinventions of the raw, distorted sound this lane is built around.
lineage: A radical solo reduction of the 'Crazy Horse fuzz' sound, one guitar and Daniel Lanois's studio treatments standing in for the whole band.

label: Reprise
description: A covers record reworking old folk standards and songbook staples ('Oh Susannah,' 'Clementine,' 'This Land Is Your Land') as full-volume Crazy Horse jams, treating nursery-rhyme-familiar songs like unreleased Ragged Glory outtakes. It is a strange, funny, sometimes genuinely unsettling record, closing with a lumbering 'God Save the Queen.' It reunited the classic Crazy Horse lineup and set up the same-year Psychedelic Pill.
lineage: Old-time American folk songs run through the Crazy Horse fuzz machine, tying this lane's Crazy Horse sound directly back to the pre-1965 folk roots the whole atlas traces to.
key_tracks: God Save the Queen/America the Beautiful

label: Reprise
description: A sprawling double album recorded right after Americana with the same reunited Crazy Horse lineup, opening with the 27-minute jam 'Driftin' Back,' one of the longest tracks Young ever released. It is the fullest, most unhurried expression of the Crazy Horse fuzz-and-feedback sound in his late catalog, songs given room to wander for ten or twenty minutes at a stretch. A late-period high point for listeners who want the band at full length.
lineage: The 2010s peak of the classic four-piece Crazy Horse sound, letting the band's long-solo instincts run further than almost any record since Ragged Glory.

label: Reprise
description: Crazy Horse's first studio album in seven years and the first to feature Nils Lofgren on guitar in place of the retired Frank Sampedro, recorded high in the Colorado Rockies. It splits between long, fuzzy jams ('She Showed Me Love' stretches past thirteen minutes) and gentler, more overtly environmentalist songwriting. It reads as a late-career reaffirmation of the classic sound after Young's mostly solo and archival 2010s output.
lineage: The reunion record that brought Nils Lofgren, who first played with Young back on After the Gold Rush, into the Crazy Horse guitar chair.

label: Reprise
description: Recorded live off the floor inside a restored 19th-century log barn in the Colorado Rockies, using the room's natural sound instead of studio reverb, this is Crazy Horse leaning fully into the live-in-the-room ethic that has run through their records since Ragged Glory. It was accompanied by a documentary film of the sessions. Songs like 'Song of the Seasons' mix accordion into the usual guitar-heavy sound, giving the record a slightly rustic, campfire edge.
lineage: A late-period return to the barn-recorded, live-off-the-floor method Young and Crazy Horse first used on Ragged Glory three decades earlier.

label: Reprise
description: Co-produced with Rick Rubin, this Crazy Horse record leans into environmental and personal themes across loose, warm arrangements. It is less about volume than mood, a mellower late-period Crazy Horse record than Barn or Colorado, closer in spirit to the reflective side of Harvest Moon than to Ragged Glory's roar. It continued the string of albums the Lofgren-era lineup put out in the early 2020s.
lineage: A Rick Rubin-produced late-period Crazy Horse record, mellower than Barn or Colorado but continuing the same reunited lineup's run of 2020s albums.

label: Reprise
description: A secret November 2023 club show at Toronto's tiny Rivoli, where Crazy Horse played Ragged Glory front to back for an audience of a few hundred, released the following spring as a Record Store Day live album with songs retitled from lyric fragments. It's a loose, sweaty, low-stakes document, the opposite of an arena spectacle, and it plays like the band checking in on a thirty-four-year-old record to see if the fuzz still holds up. It does.
lineage: A full live run-through of Ragged Glory more than three decades later, with Talbot and Molina revisiting the album most identified with the 'Crazy Horse fuzz' sound.

artist: Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts
label: Reprise
description: Young's first album with a new backing band, the Chrome Hearts (Micah Nelson on guitar, Spooner Oldham on keys, plus a rhythm section), continuing the same ragged, plainspoken songwriting this lane is built on. 'Family Life' and the pointed protest song 'Big Change' set distorted guitar and blunt lyrics side by side, much as Crazy Horse records have for decades. It is the newest entry in a lineage that runs back to Buffalo Springfield.
lineage: A new backing band, the Chrome Hearts, sounding like it has stepped into the role Crazy Horse has long occupied, keeping the ragged-guitar, cracked-voice sound going into a new decade.

label: Reprise
description: Recorded solo acoustic in Toronto in January 1971, right between After the Gold Rush and Harvest, and held in the vault for 36 years before release in Young's Archives Performance Series. It captures early versions of 'Old Man' and 'Heart of Gold' before they appeared on Harvest, along with songs played solo on guitar and piano. A between-albums snapshot of the quiet, country-folk half of Young's sound at its most intimate.
lineage: An archival release (recorded 1971, released 2007) capturing Young solo and acoustic between After the Gold Rush and Harvest, with early versions of songs that would define both records.
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded live in Toronto in January 1971, officially released in 2007; logged under its 2007 release year per assignment instructions.

label: Reprise
description: Drawn from six solo shows at a small Washington, D.C. club in late 1970, this archival release captures Young alone on guitar and piano just before Harvest, including an early solo reading of 'Old Man' cut before the song had a full-band arrangement. It's a quieter, more intimate companion to Live at Massey Hall 1971, recorded only weeks apart, and it fills in another piece of the gap between After the Gold Rush and Harvest. Being a small-club document rather than a concert-hall one, it has an even closer, more conversational feel between songs.
lineage: An archival release (recorded 1970, released 2013) from the same solo-acoustic period as Live at Massey Hall 1971, filling out the picture of Young between After the Gold Rush and Harvest.
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded at a Washington D.C. club in November-December 1970, officially released in 2013; logged under its 2013 release year per assignment instructions.

artist: Neil Young and the Stray Gators
label: Reprise
description: A concert recording from early in the troubled 1973 tour later documented on Time Fades Away, capturing the Stray Gators with Ben Keith's pedal steel before a drummer change and the tour's unraveling. It is a calmer, more together-sounding document than Time Fades Away, closer to how Harvest's songs were meant to sound live. Released decades later in the Archives series, it works as a companion piece showing the tour's steadier chapter.
lineage: An archival release (recorded 1973, released 2019) from the same tour as Time Fades Away, with the Stray Gators' earlier lineup, showing the country-rock side of that period before it frayed.
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded in Tuscaloosa, Alabama in February 1973, officially released in 2019; logged under its 2019 release year per assignment instructions.

label: Reprise
description: A long-shelved 1974-75 album about the end of Young's relationship with actress Carrie Snodgress, pulled from the release schedule at the last minute in favor of the harsher Tonight's the Night and left in the vault for 45 years. It is mostly acoustic and quietly devastated rather than drunk and howling, with early versions of songs like 'Star of Bethlehem' that later turned up elsewhere. Its long-delayed release closed one of the most famous gaps in his catalog.
lineage: An archival release (recorded 1974-75, released 2020), shelved originally in favor of Tonight's the Night; its gentle country-folk sound sits between Harvest and Comes a Time.
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded 1974-75, officially released in 2020 after decades on the shelf; logged under its 2020 release year per assignment instructions.

label: Reprise
description: A single-session solo acoustic album cut in one night in August 1976 with producer David Briggs, with Young running through early, spare versions of songs that would later appear on Rust Never Sleeps, American Stars 'n Bars and other records. The close, minimal recording makes it feel like sitting in the room with him. It works almost like a Rosetta Stone for a stretch of Young's mid-1970s songwriting, showing the bare bones under songs such as 'Powderfinger.'
lineage: An archival release (recorded 1976, released 2017) showing the solo-acoustic origins of songs later released on Rust Never Sleeps, American Stars 'n Bars and other records.
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded solo in one August 1976 session, officially released in 2017; logged under its 2017 release year per assignment instructions.

label: Reprise
description: One of rock's most famous unreleased albums, assembled as an acetate in 1977 from sessions dating back to 1974 and widely bootlegged for decades before Young finally issued it officially. It mixes solo acoustic tracks with full-band Crazy Horse cuts, including songs like 'Powderfinger' and 'Like a Hurricane' that fans had known from later official releases. The belated 2023 release finally let listeners hear it as sequenced.
lineage: An archival release (recorded 1974-77, released 2023) of one of the most legendary unreleased albums in rock history, sitting at the source of songs later spread across American Stars 'n Bars, Comes a Time and Rust Never Sleeps.
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded 1974-77 and shelved as an acetate, officially released in 2023; logged under its 2023 release year per assignment instructions.

label: Reprise
description: Recorded in 2000-01 during a hard stretch in Young's personal life and shelved for two decades while he released Are You Passionate? instead, this is a moody, atmospheric Crazy Horse record. It is quieter and more restrained than most Crazy Horse records, closer in mood to Sleeps with Angels or Tonight's the Night than to Ragged Glory's roar. Its long-delayed 2022 release brought a genuinely dark chapter of the band's history into daylight.
lineage: An archival release (recorded 2000-01, released 2022) documenting a somber Crazy Horse session shelved for two decades, closer in mood to Sleeps with Angels than to the band's louder records.
key_tracks: Standing in the Light of Love
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded 2000-01, officially released in 2022; logged under its 2022 release year per assignment instructions.

label: Reprise
description: An archival collection of early recordings by the original Crazy Horse lineup (Danny Whitten, Billy Talbot, Ralph Molina) from the era of Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere. It includes alternate takes and songs left off the albums of the time, offering a wider window into the band's first years before Whitten's death in 1972. For a lane built around this lineup's guitar interplay, it is a direct look at the moment the sound was first invented.
lineage: An archival release (released 2024) documenting the founding Crazy Horse lineup around the time of Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere.
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded January-October 1969 during the Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere sessions, officially released in 2024; logged under its 2024 release year per assignment instructions.

label: Reprise
description: Another long-shelved album from the extremely prolific 1974-77 stretch, mixing relaxed acoustic songs with a loose, countryish backing band, sitting alongside Homegrown and the official Chrome Dreams as one more piece of the vault Young spent the 2020s finally opening. Several of its songs had already surfaced elsewhere in different versions, so this release functions mainly as a snapshot of how they were originally sequenced and arranged. It's a minor entry next to Homegrown or Chrome Dreams, but it rounds out a remarkably clear picture of just how much material Young was sitting on during that period.
lineage: An archival release (recorded 1977, released 2025) from the same prolific mid-70s vault as Homegrown and Chrome Dreams, filling in yet another piece of that period's songwriting.
borderline_note: Archival release: recorded May-December 1977, officially released in 2025; logged under its 2025 release year per assignment instructions.
